summary:
Auto-Farm turns NASA Earth observations into the next planting decision a farmer can
actually act on. The app opens on a real satellite map of a farm in Constanza,
Dominican Republic, and answers three questions in plain language: what to plant, when
to irrigate and what climate risk the farm carries. It compares three rotation
strategies (the current crop and two alternatives) side by side, each with the
reasoning, the NASA evidence behind it, declared gaps and the risks that still need an
agronomist to review. NASA data is read at farm scale and the uncertainty is shown, not
hidden: NASA POWER reanalysis for 42 years of climate trends and risk indicators,
SRTM terrain, MODIS NDVI and GPM IMERG rainfall. A real Telegram bot (Elio) answers
questions from the farm's own data and says "I don't have that data" instead of
guessing. It matters because farmers decide with last year's weather; this gives them a
defensible, auditable decision from a phone.
details:
Farmers decide with last year's weather. Auto-Farm gives them a farm-level decision

they can read from a phone. The app opens on a real satellite map of the farm with six

demo plots, a real Telegram bot, and a monitoring panel in plain language

("127 L/m²" instead of "126.8 mm", "green 65 out of 100" instead of "NDVI 0.65").

NASA data in the product: NASA POWER reanalysis for 42 years of climate trends

(Sen + Mann-Kendall with FDR correction over 2,592 grid cells), farm climatology, and

risks (days ≥35 °C, heavy rain, dry days, frost, root-zone moisture,

evapotranspiration); SRTM elevation and slope as an erosion-risk proxy; MODIS/Terra

NDVI and GPM IMERG rainfall from NASA GIBS for the farm's pixel. Local soil comes from

ISRIC SoilGrids (clearly marked as non-NASA), and recent weather from ERA5/Open-Meteo

(also labelled non-NASA).

The core deliverable is the rotation comparison: current crop, alternative 1 and

alternative 2, with score, rationale, NASA evidence, benefits (e.g. legumes fixing

nitrogen), declared information gaps and risks to review with an agronomist. Farmer

priorities (water saving vs diversification) and a rainfall scenario slider make the

trade-offs visible. The model explains uncertainty (confidence intervals, adjusted

p-values) and why a satellite pixel is not a ground sensor.

What is simulated is labelled as simulated: sensors, roof and camera. What is missing

is declared, not hidden: bare-field calendar, pest cycles, local market and crop

parameters still need agronomic validation. This is a support tool, not a replacement

for farmer judgment.

Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript (three.js vendored locally, no CDN), Python for the

data pipelines (NASA POWER, NASA GIBS, SRTM, ISRIC SoilGrids, ERA5), a Cloudflare Worker

for the always-on assistant, and Playwright plus unittest for the test suite (192 Python

tests, 6 Node checks, CI on every push).

Demo: https://kirixdj.github.io/tierra/web/ · Code: https://github.com/KIRIXDJ/tierra
dataRefs: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) — 42-year climate trends, climatology and farm risk indicators
SRTM 1 arc-second (NASA/USGS, LP DAAC) — elevation and slope
MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices 16-day L3 Global 250 m (MOD13Q1 v061)
NASA GIBS — imagery service used to fetch the clipped NDVI and IMERG layers
projectRefs: ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0 — soil texture, organic carbon and pH (not NASA, CC BY 4.0)
Open-Meteo — last 30 days and farm forecast API (ERA5-Land)
ECMWF ERA5 — reanalysis behind the recent-weather data
Esri World Imagery — real satellite base map of the farm
Wikimedia Commons — cassava field photo (PJeganathan, CC BY-SA 4.0)
Wikimedia Commons — irrigated bean field (T. F. B. de Oliveira, CC BY 3.0)
AWS Open Data Terrain Tiles (SRTM tiles used for the slope)
DeepSeek API — runtime AI of the assistant Elio (SI)
Edge TTS — English voiceover of the 30-second demo (SI audio)
Playwright — browser tests and screen captures
Cloudflare Workers — always-on assistant for the published demo
Pillow — image processing for the satellite clips
